title: Marie Brizard Wine & Spirits returns to French growth
summary:
Marie Brizard Wine & Spirits (MBWS) has posted a 6% like-for-like rise in French sales for the second quarter, helped by the performance of William Peel whisky.

The post Marie Brizard Wine & Spirits returns to French growth appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Marie Brizard Wine & Spirits (MBWS) has posted a 6% like-for-like rise in French sales for the second quarter, helped by the gradual return of William Peel to retail shelves, new agency brand deals and a fresh Cognac industrial services contract.

The Euronext-listed company has reported group revenues of €84.0 million for the first half of 2026, down 4.4% like-for-like (down 3.0% as reported) on the same period last year, as a recovering French business only partly offset continued weakness in several international markets. The Charenton-le-Pont-based group, whose portfolio includes William Peel, Sobieski, Marie Brizard and Cognac Gautier, said second-quarter trading painted a more encouraging story: group revenues of €45.3 million were up 0.5% like-for-like (up 2.2% as reported), with France returning to clear growth after a difficult 2025.

France retail recovery

The France cluster generated H1 revenues of €35.6 million, up 1.2% like-for-like, accelerating to 6.0% growth in the second quarter alone (€18.6 million). MBWS attributed the improvement to a combination of a one-off catch-up effect and what it described as more structural gains. The off-trade channel was still down 4.0% for the half, a legacy of William Peel's 2025 delistings – the Scotch saw shelf space decline last year following MBWS price increases to cover rising inflation and maturation costs. However, the channel turned positive in Q2, up 3.8%, as the brand's gradual return to shelves took hold. Marie Brizard and Sobieski both delivered second-quarter growth on the back of product development, while new rum agency brand contracts added a further contribution. On-trade sales were the standout performer, up 10.1% over the half and 16% in the second quarter, driven by Marie Brizard innovations and a new rum agency brand distribution agreement. A Cognac industrial services contract that came into force at the end of 2025 also supported growth in the quarter, which the group noted came "against the backdrop of a continuously declining Cognac market."

Easing of international decline

The international cluster remained the weaker half of the business, with H1 revenues of €48.4 million, down 8.3% like-for-like (down 5.8% as reported). The rate of decline eased notably in the second quarter, to 3.1% like-for-like (down just 0.3% as reported). MBWS said the improvement reflected a mix of one-off catch-up effects – including Spanish industrial services returning to capacity after Q1 technical shutdowns, more favourable order phasing for Gautier in Martinique and Guadeloupe, and a US importer spreading its stock reduction over a longer period – alongside genuine structural progress, including innovation across its 'international strategic brands', growth for Marie Brizard in the US, and the integration of a newly acquired distributor in Denmark.

Challenges and growth opportunities

Looking ahead, MBWS flagged direct exposure to two live conflicts. It said the unresolved situation in the Middle East is fuelling inflation in input and transport costs across maritime and land logistics, energy and raw materials, and disrupting supply chains through longer lead times and order-collection delays. Separately, the group said the war in Ukraine could continue to affect the trading of its subsidiaries in the country and the wider region – a risk already visible in Lithuania's export figures this half. On William Peel specifically, MBWS said the brand's gradual return to some off-trade shelves since late 2025 is expected to continue, with the group "striving to boost distribution levels and market share" to build on the second half of 2025, which it described as sluggish. Strategically, the group pointed to four priorities: targeted innovation across its international strategic brands and 'flagship regional brands'; expansion of its agency brands portfolio through new French contracts; the integration of its Danish distributor acquisition; and new industrial services partnerships in France and Brazil. MBWS said it continues to actively pursue "suitable and profitable growth opportunities, both organic and external."

title: Hugo Spritz overtakes Aperol Spritz in UK summer Google searches
summary:
The Hugo Spritz has edged ahead of Aperol Spritz in UK summer Google searches for the first time, according to new data. Jessica Mason looks at what this means for the elderflower-flavoured movement.

The post Hugo Spritz overtakes Aperol Spritz in UK summer Google searches appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
The Hugo Spritz has edged ahead of Aperol Spritz in UK summer Google searches for the first time, according to new data. Jessica Mason looks at what this means for the elderflower-flavoured movement. In a new analysis of Google Trends UK web search data during the 13 weeks ending 12 July, the term Hugo Spritz recorded average indexed interest of 55.8, compared with 53.9 for Aperol Spritz, showing that the term averaged approximately 3.6% higher.

Increased curiosity

The data, which looked across comparable 13-week spring and summer periods between 2022 and 2026 highlighted that back in 2022 Hugo generated approximately 2.3% of Aperol’s average indexed interest, showing a marked increase in curiosity. Google Trends data represents normalised relative interest rather than absolute search volumes, sales or market share, however, ahead of National Spritz Day (Saturday 1 August) and with spritz recipe searches having recently doubled year on year, Britain’s love affair with lighter tasting summer serves continues unabated. In fact, searches for “spritz recipe” and “Hugo Spritz” have both doubled year on year and the spritz is now the number-one summer cocktail choice among British 18–29-year-olds while 37% of the same age group say they are socialising earlier than they were a year ago. The figure rises to 42% among 30–44-year-olds. Five years ago, the Hugo Spritz generated just a fraction of the UK Google search interest attracted by Aperol Spritz; however this new shift reflects Britain’s growing appetite for spritzes more broadly.

Growing the brand

Speaking to the drinks business about whether the St-Germain brand could or would soon be extended by its owner Bacardi across new formats such as highly popular RTDs and pre-mixed cocktails, St-Germain global vice president Emma Fox said: "The success we're seeing with St‑Germain today means our priority remains growing the core brand and continuing to recruit consumers into the category through serves such as the Hugo Spritz. There remains significant opportunity to inspire consumers with the versatility of the brand across a wide range of cocktail occasions. We continually evaluate opportunities for the future, but we have no innovation announcements to make at this time." However, Fox admitted that "the RTD category continues to grow as consumers look for premium, convenient options for a variety of social occasions. At the same time, we're seeing exceptional momentum behind the Hugo Spritz and growing interest in St‑Germain as more consumers discover the cocktail's fresh, floral and refreshing profile".

Effortless

Fox told db that "one of the strengths of St‑Germain is that it allows consumers to effortlessly create elevated serves with just a few simple ingredients, whether at home or when entertaining friends" and pointed out that while Bacardi will "continuously explore opportunities to evolve the brand and meet changing consumer needs" it has "no announcements to make regarding RTD products at this time". The analysis however already shows that interest is also expanding beyond the traditional bitter-orange serve of Aperol, with Google search trends uncovering growing curiosity around elderflower, rose, peach, frozen and non-alcoholic spritz variations, highlighting consumers’ appetite for a wider range of flavours and formats. Indeed, as St-Germain has become a key ingredient for the serve, this has had a halo effect on the brand’s popularity with UK sales of St-Germain more than doubling over the last year. Describing the boost in interest for Hugo Spritzes, St-Germain global brand ambassador Franck Dedieu said: “The Hugo Spritz has become the drink of the summer because it captures exactly how people want to socialise now. It’s lighter tasting and easy to enjoy over long lunches, garden gatherings and relaxed early-evening drinks that feel effortless but still special.”

Elegant

Dedieu explained: “Its signature floral character comes from St-Germain, made with fresh, handpicked elderflowers from France. Combined with sparkling wine, soda water, mint and lime, it creates a bright cocktail that is elegant but incredibly simple to make at home.” He added: “National Spritz Day is the perfect excuse to gather friends, fill a glass with ice and celebrate one of the defining drinks of the summer.” To find out more about how to make the perfect Hugo Spritz, read more from db here.

title: #WeekInPictures: Bodrum cocktails, English wine and whisky at The Game Fair
summary:
This week brought Federico Penzo’s Bodrum-inspired drinks programme, an English wine-led summer at Coworth Park and a new bottling range from Whisky 1901. Carlsberg also entered football’s latest commercial argument with a pointed message for Gianni Infantino.

The post #WeekInPictures: Bodrum cocktails, English wine and whisky at The Game Fair appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
This week brought Federico Penzo’s Bodrum-inspired drinks programme, an English wine-led summer at Coworth Park and a new bottling range from Whisky 1901. Carlsberg also entered football’s latest commercial argument with a pointed message for Gianni Infantino.

Bodrum Edition returned to local flavours

With Bodrum hotels at around 90% occupancy this July according to Bodrum vice-president Alişir Şahin, Bodrum Edition has united its bars under Federico Penzo’s “Back to Roots” programme. The former London bartender’s Satsuma Smash freezes Bodrum mandarin fruit and extracts oils separately, then reunites them with gin, cucumber, lime and salted sour plum.

English wine took centre stage at Coworth Park

Head Sommelier Nikos Emner has put English wine at the heart of Tide’s second summer at Coworth Park, with Rathfinny magnums poured by the glass from a branded trolley. Meanwhile, Peter Keane’s cocktail programme uses estate honey, meadow hay and apple marigold, alongside blood orange, basil and English sake. Chef Adam Smith’s Woven team serves Friday to Sunday lunches al fresco until 23 August, including a raw scallop from Britain’s only freediving scallop company.

Carlsberg addressed football’s private equity debate

Carlsberg responded to plans by football’s global governing body to sell a private equity stake in its commercial operations with an online advertisement aimed at Gianni Infantino. “Time for a hydration break, Gianni? Probably,” read the post, adapting the brewer’s familiar tagline to argue that supporters should remain central to the game.

Whisky 1901 poured at The Game Fair

Independent bottler Whisky 1901 presented its portfolio at The Game Fair at Ragley Hall in Warwickshire, welcoming whisky drinkers from the UK and overseas. Master of whisky Matt Chambers led tastings of the newly launched Ledger Series, a collection of individual casks selected to reflect the provenance and character of established Scottish distilleries. The range formed part of Whisky 1901’s attempt to give independent bottling a polished presentation without losing sight of the spirit’s origins.

Kamara unveiled new Eastern Mediterranean summer cocktails

London bar Kamara launched a new summer menu built around six months of in-house fermentation, maceration and distillation, continuing its focus on Eastern Mediterranean flavours and traditional production techniques. Created by group bar manager Marco Luisetto and general manager Zinio Fernande, the menu includes serves such as Bread + Butter, inspired by Greek tsoureki, alongside Tomato + Cucumber, Shiso + Mint and Carrot + Meadowsweet. The programme also features a collaboration with The Lost Explorer tequila and mezze dishes designed to complement the drinks, with Cretan clay vessels used throughout production to add texture and subtle mineral character.

title: Lion Brewery returns to India after six decades
summary:
A Singapore-based brewery with roots dating back to the 19th Century has returned to India after more than 60 years, launching two beers in Delhi as it seeks to jump into the country's growing premium drinks market.

The post Lion Brewery returns to India after six decades appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
A Singapore-based brewery with roots dating back to the 19th Century has returned to India after more than 60 years, launching two beers in Delhi as it seeks to jump into the country's growing premium drinks market. Lion Brewery Co, founded in London in 1836 and now headquartered in Singapore, has introduced its Island Lager and Pale Ale in Delhi through an exclusive distribution partnership with Copperdrop Spirits. The beers are available in 330ml bottles, with the company planning to expand into the neighbouring states of Haryana and Uttar Pradesh before entering other Indian cities. The great return toasts a symbolic moment for the brewer, whose history is closely linked to the origins of India Pale Ale (IPA). During the 19th Century, British breweries developed heavily hopped pale ales that could withstand the long sea voyage to India, then part of the British Empire. Lion Brewery Co was among the companies exporting beer to the subcontinent during that period, contributing to the global popularity of the IPA style. The original Lion Brewery operated on the banks of the River Thames before it ceased operating in London. Lion Brewery Co brand was revived in Singapore in 2018 and has since expanded into international markets.

A vibrant market

The brewery's return comes as a growing number of international beer producers seek to establish a presence in India's expanding premium alcohol market, where younger urban consumers are increasingly experimenting with imported and craft-style beers. India's beer market has grown rapidly in recent years, with industry estimates valuing it at around $4.5bn (£3.4bn) in 2023. The craft beer sector in particular is touted to hit US$1 billion by 2027 in what has been described as the market's "growth phase," with climbing incomes and shifting consumer tastes fuelling a thirst for higher-end products. Lion Brewery said Delhi had been chosen as the starting point for its return because of its established premium beer market. Copperdrop Spirits, the exclusive importer and distributor for India, said demand for premium international beer brands had been increasing among Indian consumers.

India's beer sector surmounts challenges

Speaking about the state of the beer sector across India, United Breweries Ltd managing director and CEO Vivek Gupta told the PTI at a local event that, despite the industry remaining under “severe cost pressure” and this damaging the bottom line, he expects the category to recover and reiterated that the overall picture is “positive”. Gupta said: “The trends in the beer category are positive, driven by good reforms in states like Karnataka and Maharashtra, and also by weather”. The beer sector has faced a series of challenges including an unfavourable exchange rate weakening the rupee as well as ongoing global conflict, which leads to the price of packaging and other imported ingredients and materials increasing. Gupta said: “Right now, there is a good positive top-line momentum. At the same time, there is work being done to recover the profit erosion that has happened because of the war impact". But, he added that the beer sector in India is, otherwise, “in a good shape” and noted “we are seeing high single-digit volume growth, and of course some price-led growth as well, but primarily it is volume growth”.

title: Ningxia archaeologists unearth 2,300-year-old liquor
summary:
Archaeologists in the Ningxia Hui autonomous region of northwestern China have uncorked new insights into ancient brewing practices after unearthing residue of a 2,300-year-old grain-based alcoholic drink.

The post Ningxia archaeologists unearth 2,300-year-old liquor appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Archaeologists in the Ningxia Hui autonomous region of northwestern China have uncorked new insights into ancient brewing practices after unearthing residue of a 2,300-year-old grain-based alcoholic drink. The cereal-based residue, discovered at the Shanjibao cemetery in Guyan city, harks back to the Warring States Period (475-221 BC), and helps experts to understand the brewing technology of Qin people who resided in the area at the time. The sample is believed to be China’s best-preserved liquid alcohol relic from the era publicly reported to date, according to the study, which appeared in the June edition of the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports. Researchers extracted the 3,740 ml liquid from inside a bronze pot with a garlic-shaped mouth – the type commonly used in the Qin era – before subjecting it to scientific analysis to determine its date of origin, according to the regional department of culture and tourism. 

Ancient understandings

Analysis of the samples, led by the Ningxia Institute of Cultural Relics and Archeology and the School of Cultural Heritage at Northwest University, revealed detailed flavour profiles, diagnostic organic acids, starches, phytoliths and yeast, providing multiple lines of evidence that helped researchers identify the ingredients and brewing techniques used to produce the alcoholic tipple. As part of the project, 183 tombs were excavated, 179 of which belonged to the Qin people. The bronze bottle belonged to Tomb M39, and was packaged with organic mud on the outside, and its inner walls were lined with textile fabrics; secure sealing which explains how the ancient spirit survived more than two millennia intact. Researchers prised open the seal with a scalpel and forceps, before extracting the liquor, which came out a pale, clear, blue-green colour.  The study found that the Qin people had already mastered the use of grain-based fermentation starters, enabling saccharification and fermentation to occur simultaneously – an indication of the sophisticated brewing techniques they had developed for the period.

title: Endeavour Group to offload Australian wine assets
summary:
Endeavour Group is selling off most of its winery assets, including Chapel Hill Estate in Australia's McLaren Vale, as part of a restructuring that will see the company focus on "brands and regions that generate the strongest returns", it announced yesterday. db reports.

The post Endeavour Group to offload Australian wine assets appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Endeavour Group is selling off most of its winery assets, including Chapel Hill Estate in Australia's McLaren Vale, as part of a restructuring that will see the company focus on "brands and regions that generate the strongest returns", it announced yesterday. db reports. Endeavour Group, which acquired Chapel Hill Estate just seven years ago, announced yesterday that while it intends to keep the wine brand it is selling off Chapel Hill's physical assets including its vineyards and cellar door. Looking for a buyer for the property, Endeavour intimated that the estate does not have to be kept for wine production. "Whether envisaged as a luxury tourism destination, hospitality venture, accommodation retreat, events venue, lifestyle estate, agritourism enterprise or the continuation of wine production, the estate provides incoming owners with the flexibility to shape its next chapter around their own vision and objectives," reads the listing. Chapel Hill, which includes an on-site heritage chapel built in 1865, has 13.69 hectares of established vineyard and a 23ML water licence. The listing also details the property's "extensive winery and warehousing infrastructure", representing "a rare opportunity to secure a fully developed property of genuine scale and significance".

Big hopes

Endeavour Drinks, a subsidiary of Australian supermarket chain Woolworths, bought Chapel Hill, known for its Shiraz and Grenache-based wines, in 2019 for an undisclosed sum. At the time it had big plans for the producer, folding Chapel Hill into Endeavour's new wine division, Paragon Wine Estates, where it would join brands including Krondorf (Barossa Valley), Isabel Estate (Marlborough) and Riddoch (Coonawarra). “Welcoming Chapel Hill to the group has inspired the creation of Paragon Wine Estates and is an exciting new element of our diverse Pinnacle Drinks business," managing director of Endeavour Drinks, Steve Donohue, said at the time. “These great wine producers deserve special attention. Each one has a rich history and unique traditions which form the basis of their wonderful stories. We hope to share those stories with wine lovers the world over.”

Company restructure

However, on Wednesday 30 July Endeavour Group (EDG) announced it was selling off the lion's share of its winery and vineyard assets as part of a AU$300 million cost-saving strategy led by new managing director and CEO Jayne Hrdlicka. Described by the Sydney-based company as a “strategic transformation”, the restructure aims to boost profitability by focusing on "brands and regions that generate the strongest returns", while "exiting or selling non-core winery and agricultural assets". As db has reported, Australian wine regions are facing catastrophic losses, leading to the country's wine exports dropping to a 22-year low, according to Wine Australia. Australia also posted its lowest wine harvest for 25 years – the result of weak global demand and severe weather conditions. At 1.27m tonnes, the total 2026 crush slid 19% on 2025, and is around 25% below the decade average, laying bare the pressures facing producers. The value of the vintage has also plummeted, dropping 26% to AU$837 million (£433 million).

Who stays and who goes?

Endeavour plans to retain the Chapel Hill, Riddoch and Krondorf brands, although their physical assets will be sold to meet the company's goal of an 80% reduction in its own grape growing, instead moving to a model of "99% flexible sourcing of purchased bulk wine and grapes". Yarra Valley winery Oakridge and Tasmanian winery Josef Chromy are also for the chop. Cape Mentelle in Margaret River and Dorrien Estate in the Barossa Valley are the only Australian wineries that Endeavour will retain in full, alongside Isobel Estates in Marlborough, New Zealand. "By concentrating on the brands and assets that customers value most, we are building a more focused private label portfolio," said Hrdlicka.

title: Harrison Ford co-creates Glenmorangie whisky for global travel retail
summary:
Glenmorangie has unveiled a limited-edition single malt created in collaboration with Harrison Ford, with the Highland distillery rolling out the exclusive bottling across international airports as it builds on its Formula 1 partnership and global travel retail ambitions.

The post Harrison Ford co-creates Glenmorangie whisky for global travel retail appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Glenmorangie has unveiled a limited-edition single malt created in collaboration with Harrison Ford, with the Highland distillery rolling out the exclusive bottling across international airports as it builds on its Formula 1 partnership and global travel retail ambitions. Glenmorangie has released a limited-edition whisky developed alongside Harrison Ford, marking the first time the Hollywood actor has collaborated directly on the creation of a bottling for the Highland distillery. The Glenmorangie Harrison Ford Limited Edition has launched exclusively through selected travel retail locations, where Moët Hennessy Travel Retail is supporting the release with dedicated airport activations designed to increase the brand's visibility among international travellers. Rather than simply lending his name to the release, Ford worked alongside Glenmorangie's director of whisky creation, Dr Bill Lumsden MBE, to develop a whisky reflecting his own flavour preferences.

From campaign star to whisky collaborator

The collaboration grew out of Glenmorangie's Once Upon a Time in Scotland campaign, which featured Ford visiting the distillery in the Scottish Highlands. According to the company, Lumsden introduced the actor to a range of cask samples before the pair refined the final recipe over several months by exchanging whisky samples across the Atlantic. The finished whisky combines Glenmorangie's signature bourbon cask maturation with a parcel of spirit finished in toasted Portuguese red wine casks, producing flavours including citrus, apricot, muscovado sugar and butter candy before a finish of orange oil, leather and oak tannins. It is bottled at 46.5% ABV and carries a recommended retail price of €90 (US$100). Ford said: "I loved my time at Glenmorangie and have enormous respect for the team at the Distillery. They are true craftspeople." He added: "Collaborating with Dr Bill was a real treat, a chance to get inside the mind of a maker who combines art and science to create incredible single malt Scotch whisky... The Glenmorangie Harrison Ford Limited Edition is everything I want in a whisky. I'm immensely proud of our creation." Lumsden described Ford as "an honorary member of our Whisky Creation Team", adding that the whisky combined Glenmorangie's signature elegance with "the tang and structure of toasted Portuguese red wine casks".

Travel retail focus

To support the launch, Moët Hennessy Travel Retail is introducing immersive activation spaces in airports around the world, featuring whisky tastings, cocktail serves and storytelling designed to recreate elements of the Scottish Highlands for travellers. The release is accompanied by a new instalment of Once Upon a Time in Scotland, filmed in Ford's home state of Wyoming, in which the actor tastes the finished whisky for the first time before delivering his understated verdict: "It's nice. It's very nice."

Building on Formula 1 partnership

As previously reported by the drinks business, Glenmorangie became the Official Whisky of Formula 1 last year as part of LVMH's decade-long partnership with the championship, joining Moët & Chandon, TAG Heuer and Louis Vuitton among the luxury group's brands with a presence in the sport. The Harrison Ford collaboration forms part of Glenmorangie's wider push to increase its global profile through high-profile partnerships and premium travel retail, where limited-edition releases continue to play an increasingly important role in attracting collectors and international consumers.

title: US wine industry risks losing ground without collective marketing
summary:
While regional trade organisations “do excellent work”, the US wine trade "does not do a fantastic job" of collective marketing, says agency founder behind anti-prohibitionist campaign.

The post US wine industry risks losing ground without collective marketing appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
While regional trade organisations “do excellent work”, the US wine trade "does not do a fantastic job" of collective marketing, says agency founder behind anti-prohibitionist campaign.

The US wine industry lags badly behind other agricultural sectors when it comes to funding and sustaining collective marketing, according to Gino Colangelo, founder of New York wine PR agency Colangelo & Partners, who has spent the past four years running a pro-bono campaign to counter what he described as growing anti-alcohol sentiment in American media. Speaking to The Drinks Business Podcast as his agency marks its 20th anniversary, Colangelo said he began noticing a marked rise in negative media coverage linking wine and alcohol to health harms roughly four years ago.

The beauty of wine

Conversations with wine critic and Wine Bible author Karen McNeil led to the creation of Come Over October, a campaign – now also backed by California-based wine PR figure Kimberly Charles – built around promoting wine's role in bringing people together, and its status as an agricultural, historical and food-linked product. "We're hoping this campaign becomes a movement to advocate for the beauty of wine," Colangelo said, describing the initiative as mission-driven and entirely donated time on the part of its founders. But he was candid about the difficulty of sustaining momentum without structural industry support. Unlike sectors such as dairy, almonds or cranberries – which benefit from established collective marketing bodies in the US – wine has no equivalent apparatus, he said, and described the level of backing the campaign receives from companies it aims to help as "frankly, at times a bit discouraging." He said support, activations and funding for the campaign have come in "fits and starts" rather than consistently.

Sustained marketing needed

Colangelo drew a broader lesson from wine regions and trade bodies that do invest consistently in the US market – citing Wines of Georgia, Chianti Classico, the Prosecco DOC Consortium and Chile as examples of organisations that have built market share through sustained, incremental campaigns rather than one-off pushes. In a subsequent conversation, he also stressed the “excellent work” by regional trade organizations in the US like the Paso Robles Wine Country Alliance, Finger Lakes Wine Alliance and Napa Valley Vintners. Groups that "come in with a big program and then disappear for two years," he said, typically fail to build lasting traction. He likened market presence to driving an electric car rather than a petrol one: "You take your foot off the accelerator and it stops... If you stop, you will lose your market share real fast."

Countering the headwinds

On the underlying question of whether the current US downturn is cyclical or structural, Colangelo said he believes it is fundamentally cyclical, but warned that the length and depth of the downturn depends directly on continued industry investment in marketing and advocacy. "If we're aggressive and we promote and we communicate and we advocate, then we could shorten that cycle, and the trough won't be quite as deep," he said. Come Over October and similar sector-wide advocacy efforts are likely to face continued pressure given wider headwinds, which Colangelo cited later in the conversation, including competition from THC beverages and RTDs, the rise of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, and broader "sober curious" and moderation trends among younger consumers. As previously reported on by db, Come Over October – along with Share & Pair Sundays – have become the largest pro-wine grassroots campaigns ever launched in the US – reaching just shy of 3 billion impressions in the media with another 5.6 million on social media.

title: Groove Armada launches Do It Right lager with Signature Brew
summary:
Signature Brew is teaming up with electronic music icons Groove Armada and regenerative farming pioneers Wildfarmed to launch a Czech-style lager named Do It Right. Jessica Mason reports.

The post Groove Armada launches Do It Right lager with Signature Brew appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Signature Brew is teaming up with electronic music icons Groove Armada and regenerative farming pioneers Wildfarmed to launch a Czech-style lager named Do It Right. Jessica Mason reports. After selling his music rights to buy a farm in France, Groove Armada musician Andy Cato co-founded Wildfarmed when he later moved back to the UK in 2018 and became a National Trust tenant farmer.

Beer, music, the land

The beer, Do It Right, is a three-way collaboration which bridges the gap between regenerative agriculture, music culture, and brewing. As a natural fit for the union, Signature Brew has spent more than a decade uniting people through beer, music, and live experiences from its brewery and music venue in London’s east end and the beer Do It Right has been brewed using Wildfarmed’s regeneratively farmed malted barley.  As such, the collaboration is an example of how beer can help to bring nature back to fields and support British farmers while also reminding people about what matters: the land and getting together to make a positive impact.

A movement with purpose

Wildfarmed’s network of growers all use farming practices that focus on improving soil health, increasing biodiversity, minimising water pollution and reducing carbon – allowing brewing and nature recovery to exist side-by-side. Speaking to the drinks business, Signature Brew, co-founder Tom Bott, said: "The things that unite people are becoming more important than the things that divide them. Great music, great beer and a shared belief that we should leave the land in a better place all have the power to bring people together. If a beer can help start those conversations, support regenerative farming and remind people that doing the right thing doesn't have to come at the expense of having a good time, then we've achieved something we're really proud of." Bott explained: “Brewing with Wildfarmed's regenerative malted barley gave us the opportunity to create something that's bigger than a beer collaboration. Wildfarmed exists to improve the world through better farming practices, while Signature Brew exists to make the live music experience better through exceptional beer. Bringing those two movements together to create a beer with genuine purpose makes this one of our most meaningful collaborations to date.”

'Unite people in a shared mission'

Groove Armada's Cato admitted that "it was DJing that allowed me to hang on during 10 years of experimentation in the fields, searching for ways to combine growing grains with restoring soils and nature. Back then, the farm and DJ booth felt like separate worlds. But as we built the Wildfarmed movement, I realised the two have a lot in common. Whether behind the Groove Armada turntables or talking at a Wildfarmed open day, the objective is the same - to unite people in a shared mission. It’s great to now have a beer that brings these two worlds together. There can’t be many better ways than drinking a cold lager to directly support farmers who are restoring soils and nature".

Where to buy it

The new, purpose-led 5% ABV lager Do It Right will be released nationwide across Waitrose stores in 440ml cans retailing at £3 each and will also be available in both keg and can formats across pubs, bars and venues this week. Waitrose beer and cider buyer Jourdan Gabbini added: “We are thrilled to be exclusively launching Signature Brew's Do It Right lager at Waitrose, as this is exactly what our beer-loving customers look for when it comes to high-quality, indie beers. This lager also aligns strongly with our ethics and sustainability strategies, and we are proud to stock another product which pioneers regenerative farming."

title: Italian company enters UK market by acquiring Jascots Wine Merchants
summary:
Italian food company Compagnia del Gusto Holding has acquired Jascots Wine Merchants from Freixenet Copestick, it was announced this morning.

The post Italian company enters UK market by acquiring Jascots Wine Merchants appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Italian food company Compagnia del Gusto Holding has acquired Jascots Wine Merchants from Freixenet Copestick, it was announced this morning. Compagnia del Gusto Holding will assume responsibility for the administrative and sales teams of Jascots through its UK subsidiary, CDGH UK.   The Italian holding company is not only a newcomer to the UK retail market but also a relatively new company. Founded by the Cosulich family in 2025, its main activity is the investment and development of SME food & beverage brands, focusing on “iconic brands and high-value-added niches”. Its Italian holding company comprises three operational divisions: the Compagnia del Mare, presiding over its seafood and artisanal specialties division; its wine division, Compagnia delle Vigne; and its regional food division, Compagnia dei Sapori which ranges from pasta to condiments, baked goods and artisanal desserts. It has already signalled its ambition to grow its turnover to €200 million in turnover in five years, according to Italian news outlet Il Sole 24 ORE. The acquisition marks a significant new chapter for Jascots, the company said, which would supports the scale of ambition and future potential within the business.  In addition to continuing the merchants extensive international portfolio in the on-trade, the new owners also plan to leverage its own network to bring its Italian wine and food portfolio to the UK market, as part of a strategic partnership between Compangnia del Gusto and Jascots, to strengthen their premium wine distribution capabilities across the UK on-trade sector. Freixenet Copestick and Compagnia del Gusto Holding will continue to work closely together, ensuring continuity for customers and maintaining the strong connection between Jascots and key premium brands including Bolney Wine Estate, Champagne Alfred Gratien and Schloss Johannisberg, the company confirmed. As part of the transaction, colleagues whose roles are dedicated to the Jascots business will transition to the new company, with a clear focus on ensuring continuity and supporting them responsibly throughout the process.

Milestone

Omar Raafat, head of Jascots, called it an exciting milestone for Jascots which “reflects our ambition to keep investing in our business, our customers, and our future — something that's exciting for both myself and the team to be part of.” Ettore Nicoletto, CEO of Compagnia del Gusto Holding, said the deal was also a key milestone in the Group’s international growth strategy. “The UK is a strategic market for premium Italian wines and with Jascots we gain a solid distribution platform, an experienced team and deep expertise in the on-trade. We look forward to bringing the best of our Italian portfolio to such a prestigious customer base." Freixenet Copestick rescued the well-respected merchant and wine supplier, which was founded in 1986, from administrators back in December 2020 following a very challenging year due to Covid-19. When the first lockdown was announced in March, Jascot said it sales went from 85% of its normal business to zero within a matter of days as the on-trade shuts its doors, and although it swiftly diversified into direct to consumer and independent off-trade, the market conditions had proved “insurmountable”. Damian Clarke, managing director of Freixenet Copestick & CSO of Henkell Freixenet said the team were “proud of what has been achieved with Jascots Wine Merchants” and said the acquisition would “further strengthen Jascots position in the UK On-Trade market."

title: Southern Glazer’s expands Colorado footprint with Eagle Rock acquisition
summary:
Southern Glazer's Wine & Spirits has completed its acquisition of Eagle Rock Distributing's Colorado business, further strengthening its position in the rapidly consolidating US beverage distribution sector.

The post Southern Glazer’s expands Colorado footprint with Eagle Rock acquisition appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Southern Glazer's Wine & Spirits has completed its acquisition of Eagle Rock Distributing's Colorado business, further strengthening its position in the rapidly consolidating US beverage distribution sector. Southern Glazer's Wine & Spirits has completed the acquisition of substantially all of the assets of Eagle Rock Distributing Co.'s Colorado operations, expanding its beer, spirits and non-alcoholic drinks portfolio in one of the country's fastest-growing beverage markets. The transaction gives Southern Glazer's responsibility for distributing Anheuser-Busch's portfolio in Colorado, including Michelob ULTRA, Budweiser, Bud Light and Busch Light, alongside brands such as Cutwater Spirits, NÜTRL Vodka Seltzer, BeatBox Beverages, Phorm Energy and a range of soft drinks and water brands.

Consolidation gathers pace

The acquisition is the latest example of consolidation across the US wholesale drinks sector as distributors seek greater scale and broader portfolios. Wayne E. Chaplin, president and chief executive of Southern Glazer's Wine & Spirits, said: "Closing this transaction is an important step in strengthening our total beverage capabilities in Colorado. Eagle Rock's strong portfolio, talented team, and customer relationships make this a natural fit, and we're excited to build on their success." Southern Glazer's said the acquisition strengthens its route-to-market capabilities across Colorado while expanding the range of products available to customers throughout the state. The company will continue operating from Eagle Rock's existing facilities while immediately beginning distribution of supplier products across the territory.

Leadership appointments

To oversee the enlarged Colorado business, Southern Glazer's has appointed Jeffrey Gerali as senior vice president and general manager of Southern Glazer's Beverage Company of Colorado. Gerali joins from Anheuser-Busch, where he most recently served as senior commercial director, having previously held sales leadership roles at PepsiCo. Jason Charboneau has also been appointed senior vice president of sales for the Colorado operation after previously leading the beer and non-alcoholic division at Southern Glazer's Beverage Company of Nevada. Mark Chaplin, president of commercial sales at Southern Glazer's, said: "This acquisition enhances our ability to serve customers with a broader portfolio across key growth categories. Together with Eagle Rock's strong market presence, we're well positioned to create new opportunities for suppliers and customers throughout Colorado." Mike Economos, president of Eagle Rock Distributing Co., added: "We're proud of the business our Colorado team has built and are confident Southern Glazer's is the right organisation to carry it forward. Their scale, expertise, and commitment to partnership will support continued success in the market for suppliers and customers."

Industry reshaping

The deal comes as the US wholesale drinks industry continues to undergo significant restructuring. As previously reported by the drinks business, Republic National Distributing Company (RNDC) recently entered Chapter 11 proceedings after months of selling operations across multiple states, with the distributor confirming that interested parties are continuing discussions over the acquisition of its remaining markets.

title: Anishka Jelicich starts as New Zealand Winegrowers CEO
summary:
Anishka Jelicich has pledged to “listen, learn and spend time with people across the industry,” as she begins in her new role as CEO of New Zealand Winegrowers (NZW), following an international wine career spanning more than two decades.

The post Anishka Jelicich starts as New Zealand Winegrowers CEO appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Anishka Jelicich has pledged to “listen, learn and spend time with people across the industry,” as she begins in her new role as CEO of New Zealand Winegrowers (NZW), following an international wine career spanning more than two decades. Jelicich replaces Philip Gregan, who spent 24 years at the helm of the organisation, steering the ship of New Zealand's wine sector through successful eras and challenging periods like the devastating aftermath of Cyclone Gabrielle, before stepping down in June. “We are very pleased to have Anishka join us as CEO,” said NZW chair Fabian Yukich, commenting on Jelicich’s new position. “She brings a deep understanding of the New Zealand wine industry, combined with extensive global experience and strong leadership capability. Her strategic perspective and ability to build alignment across stakeholders will be invaluable as we navigate both the opportunities and challenges ahead for our sector.” Jelicich takes on the role from her former Paris-based position as global director of responsible marketing and sales for French wine and spirits company Pernod Ricard. The native New Zealander has moved to Auckland to work out of NZW’s head office.  Reflecting on her new role, Jelicich said: “Having spent much of my career working internationally in the global wine and drinks sector, I've had the privilege of seeing New Zealand wine through the eyes of the world. Time and again I've seen the extraordinary respect our wines, our people and our industry command globally.  “That perspective has only deepened a connection that is both personal and professional, making it a real privilege to join an organisation that has helped shape one of New Zealand's great success stories through the leadership of Philip Gregan, the NZW Board, the NZW team, our members and those who have contributed over many years.”

Understanding what matters most

Looking ahead, she added: “Today, New Zealand wine is the country's eighth largest export, generating approximately NZ$2.1 billion annually, with our distinctive, refreshing and sustainable wines enjoyed by consumers in more than 100 markets around the world.  “My first priority is therefore to listen, learn and spend time with people across the industry, understanding what matters most before we write the next chapter together.” In an exclusive interview with the drinks business just months before he steps down, Gregan revealed that he was  “looking forward to the change” of retirement. “I’ve had a hugely enjoyable involvement in the industry for over 40 years but it is time to step back,” he said, before admitting he doesn’t have any firm plans for what comes next. “I have listened to advice from colleagues to take my time before deciding,” he added. In this time in the trade, Gregan witnessed the astonishing rise of New Zealand wine from having “practically no level of recognition in international markets” to exporting 288.772 million litres of wine in 2025, according to the latest New Zealand Winegrowers Annual Report. “When I joined the wine industry in 1983, we were a small domestically-focused industry, with only about 100 wineries and less than 5,000 ha of grapes,” he told db. “Back then, fortified wines were still a huge part of the sector, something that is virtually non-existent today. We now export $NZ 2.1 billion worth of wine to more than 100 countries.”

title: How heatwaves affect what we drink
summary:
As another heatwave begins in Europe, you might think all this dry, sunny weather would benefit drinks sales. We consider the impact on wine, and which styles stand to benefit.

The post How heatwaves affect what we drink appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
As another heatwave begins in Europe, you might think all this dry, sunny weather would benefit drinks sales. We consider if that's true, as well as the impact on wine, and which styles stand to benefit.

While the heat and drought have brought renewed focus to climate change's impact on wine production – not least the devastating wildfires in France and Spain – rather less has been said about the weather's effect on consumption. Yet sunny conditions clearly influence what people drink, as well as what they eat.

A shift toward cold-served wine

In the UK, news surfaced during the first heatwave in late May that sales of salad had surged, while db noted last summer that temperatures ranging from 20°C to 26°C had seen consumers drop red and white wine in favour of rosé.

Certainly, a general trend in global consumption has seen a move away from reds, and towards sparkling, white and rosé wines. Until recently, the world drank more red than white and rosé combined, but red's share has now fallen below 50%.

Add orange wines to that mix – another growth area, if still a niche category – and all these styles share one thing in common: they are served cold.

As bright spots in an otherwise declining global wine market, one must assume their resilience owes something to the refreshment they offer, particularly during the more regular spells of extended hot weather now affecting Europe.

How producers are responding

The impact has been varied. For some producers, the shift away from red wine consumption has prompted them to make rosé from existing red vineyards, while others have experimented with blanc de noirs – white wines made from red grapes such as Malbec (Trivento) and Cabernet (Changyu Moser XV). Some may be grafting over or replanting red vineyards with white varieties altogether.

Large-scale vineyard removals have also taken place, particularly in red-focused Chile and Bordeaux, which have each uprooted nearly 30,000 hectares over the past three years. Both regions are now looking to reposition themselves.

Chile is promoting the crisp whites and lighter reds from its cooler Pacific-facing vineyards under the Chile Pacífico banner, highlighting fresh Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir and coastal seafood pairings – a notable shift for a country better known for Carmenère and steak straight from the asado.

Bordeaux, meanwhile, is promoting "chillable" reds, reviving its historic "claret" name for a new generation of lighter, fruit-forward wines designed to be served cold and appeal to younger consumers. Whether the strategy succeeds remains to be seen, although major brands including Calvet and Mouton Cadet have already embraced the concept.

Testing the theory: what collectors want

To test whether warmer weather is genuinely altering tastes among collectors, iDealwine is repeating its climate-focused consumer survey this autumn. Co-founder Angélique de Lencquesaing believes hotter summers are already influencing the fine wine market. As she tells db in a recent podcast, Burgundy may remain the leading beneficiary, but she also expects growing demand for refreshing whites such as Chenin Blanc and Riesling, alongside lighter reds based on Cabernet Franc and Grenache.

The last time the online auction business ran such a survey, it found warmer weather was already affecting customers' buying decisions. While only a minority (18%) said they would choose a different variety in an attempt to source lower-ABV wines, as much as 45% admitted to seeking out more white wine in future, while 74% said they favoured older vintages as temperatures rose, viewing them as more balanced than younger, hotter-year wines.

The UK's 'feta fatigue'

In sharp contrast, however, last week – following the July heatwave – UK supermarket Waitrose released figures showing a spike in sales of South African red wine alongside cottage pie, suggesting British consumers were tiring of cold drinks and light foods. The retailer dubbed the trend 'feta fatigue' and 'reverse comfort eating' – with lighthearted social commentary suggested that Brits could only manage a few days away from stodgy food and warming wines.

Clearly, forecasting what people will drink when the mercury climbs is hard to do accurately. But there's a bigger concern for anyone making and selling wine: consumers might move away from the drink altogether if temperatures continue to rise.

When beer and water win out

Indeed, some of the category's wider struggles may themselves be linked to climate: at a certain point, wine's alcohol content becomes less appealing. Lower-alcohol beverages – especially beer – and soft drinks typically gain ground during periods of extreme heat.

In France, a study of drinks consumption in the on-trade by Fyre compared sales trends during the heatwave period of 22–28 June this year with a reference week from 8–14 June. It showed water volumes increased by 36%; dairy and plant-based drinks rose by 33%; syrups and concentrates by 26%, and soft drinks by 18%.

Meanwhile, hot chocolate volumes fell by 49%, tea by 37% and coffee by 26%. Among alcoholic drinks, beer proved the most resilient, remaining almost stable at -0.3%, while wine volumes fell by 25% and spirits declined by 14%. Despite the strong growth in water and soft drinks, total beverage volumes fell by 5.5% during the heatwave week.

Although the report doesn't mention it, this downward trend may have been influenced by Paris's ban on public alcohol consumption during the most extreme point of June's heatwave (26–28 June) – though licensed bars and restaurants were exempt.

Nevertheless, the findings show that when its gets very hot, drinks sales actually decline.

Supporting such a conclusion comes with research published in March this year from the University of California, ETH Zurich and North Carolina State University, which found that alcohol sales increase with temperature up to just over 32°C before beginning to decline, partly because people are less inclined to go out.

The bigger question

As Europe's summers grow hotter, the wine trade is adapting with more cold-served and lighter styles. But if temperatures continue climbing, the bigger challenge may not be which wines consumers choose – but whether they choose wine at all.

title: Chef Q&A: Nathan Outlaw
summary:
The seafood chef and owner of Outlaw’s Bistro talks beer, closures and openings – and the need for children to understand fish. Amelie Maurice-Jones reports.

The post Chef Q&A: Nathan Outlaw appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content: The seafood chef and owner of Outlaw’s Bistro talks beer, closures and openings – and the need for children to understand fish. Amelie Maurice-Jones reports. You’ve just announced a partnership with Estrella Galicia. What made the Spanish brewery the perfect pick to partner with? Cornwall and Galicia have a synergy between them. Both have Celtic roots, both are blessed with fantastic seafood, and I’ve seen first-hand that they share the same passion as me. Lots of foods pair brilliantly with beer – but have there been any combos that have surprised you? I recently visited the Estrella Galicia brewery on a fact-finding trip. We were given a glass of 1906 Black Coupage, a beer that I’d normally expect to be served with a dessert dish. However, the chef served it with a mussel escabeche dish – and it was mind-blowing. What have been the main lessons you’ve learnt since closing your Michelin-starred flagship site, Outlaw’s New Road, in March? It’s confirmed that the customer appreciates simply but expertly cooked food, along with top-class hospitality. I’m really glad about that, because it was the intention when I made the change. What’s been the biggest positive surprise and biggest challenge since opening Outlaw’s Bistro in April? The biggest surprise has been the willingness of customers to try lesser-known species of fish, especially first-time customers who haven’t eaten with us before and don’t know what to expect. The biggest challenge has been lunch service; getting the word out to people who may not have thought about eating with us for lunch before. However, it’s a thrill when they do… and especially when they return on more occasions. What’s been your favourite ever memory with a customer? My favourite memories are all the celebrations that I’ve been privileged to witness; special birthdays, special anniversaries, weddings and such. That customers trust me and my team to serve them a meal on their special occasion that will be a treasured memory for the rest of their lives is immense. What’s the most underrated part of being a professional chef? The amount of clearing up you have to do. I do more clearing up than cooking. I was always taught that, when cooking, you clear up as you go. It’s impossible to cook well if you’re in a mess, and it drives me mad if I see someone trying to do that. I actually like taking my turn in the wash-up; it’s calming. There’s an octopus invasion in UK waters, which many fear is decimating the shellfish industry. Has this influenced your menu? I’ve always used a wide variety of seafood, so it’s not really an issue for me, but it’s impacted the wider industry immensely. I’m lucky – I have a good supply of lobsters due to being located in Port Isaac. The coastline is rocky here and, therefore, ideal for lobsters. Many put the octopus influx down to rising temperatures. How else is climate change affecting seafood chefs? I’m seeing lots more species of fish that would traditionally have only been seen in warmer waters. The most significant of these are bluefin tuna and gilthead bream, which has been very exciting. Bluefin tuna has only been around in our waters for about the last four years, and I’ve been using it for the last three. We had to adapt our way of working because of the sheer size of it and getting it into our kitchen. UK seafood consumption has fallen by 25% in the last decade. What can be done to change this? The general public needs more education about fish and seafood, and it should be starting at school level. Introducing kids to fish and seafood early would mean they’d be more likely to eat it as adults. However, they need to be taught what to look for when sourcing it, and how to cook it too. They also need to be taught about sustainability. Pick a dish from your menu, and the beer you’d pair it with. Steamed turbot and warm tartare sauce. The dish is served with crispy fried potatoes, and pairs extremely well with Estrella Galicia’s Cerveza lager. What’s something you’re currently excited about? I’m really looking forward to travelling more, both for business and pleasure. The more I see of both Britain and the rest of the world, the more I want to see.

title: Wine List of the Week: The Tudor Pass at Great Fosters
summary:
Douglas Blyde falls down the rabbit hole at The Tudor Pass in Surrey, delighting in inventive British cooking and an adventurous wine list in the remarkably well-preserved 16th century setting.

The post Wine List of the Week: The Tudor Pass at Great Fosters appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Douglas Blyde falls down the rabbit hole at The Tudor Pass in Surrey, delighting in inventive British cooking and an adventurous wine list in the remarkably well-preserved 16th century setting. Great Fosters, an SLH Hotel in Egham, has witnessed changing dynasties since Tudor times. Built around 1550 as a royal hunting lodge, the Grade I-listed house became a hotel in 1931 and joined the Alexander Hotel Collection in 2018. Its 50 acres embrace clipped parterres, a Saxon moat, ancient cedar walks and a vast, agreeably temperate outdoor swimming pool. The formal Tudor gardens are widely believed to have inspired the Queen of Hearts’ labyrinth and chess-match sequence in Walt Disney’s 1951 Alice in Wonderland. Upstairs, the Tapestry Suite, associated with Anne Boleyn during her courtship with Henry VIII, combines 17th-century Flemish tapestries, Jacobean carvings and a plaster ceiling bearing heraldic devices of the Percy family of Anne’s earlier suitor. Downstairs sits something more contemporary: a seven-table restaurant redefining itself. Reopened under Stefano Di Giosia in 2025, The Tudor Pass has retained its Michelin star while developing a clear personality. Most distinctive is Di Giosia’s determination to reinterpret not only his Italian heritage, but much beyond it, through British ingredients. Michelin advises choosing the longer menu; they are right.

Drinks

“We call it a book rather than a list,” says marketing manager Bryndal Bennett. Its author, Mantua-born sous chef Luca Delfini, took control last November and regards completion as a suspicious concept. “It’s like a baby that keeps growing,” he says. The version I saw here several years ago was simple, though not in the flattering sense. This is immeasurably more worldly.  Di Giosia’s preface describes wines which “answer from afar” to cooking rooted in place and season. Delfini has made that more than a line of copy. Armenian Voskehat, Georgian qvevri red, Japanese Koshu, Croatian Malvazija and Santorini Assyrtiko sit beside Burgundy, Bordeaux and Piedmont. A 2006 Jacques Puffeney Arbois and three vintages of Vigne Marina Coppi Timorasso, from 2014, 2017 and 2019, show curiosity about age as well as origin.  English wine is treated as a category rather than a patriotic garnish. “We have a collaboration with them,” Delfini says of Balfour. Leslie’s Reserve Brut and Rosé appear by the glass and bottle, as does Nannette’s Rosé. Chapel Down Kit’s Coty Chardonnay, meanwhile, costs £24 per 125ml and £145 per bottle: six glasses total £144, a rare instance in which ordering by the glass carries virtually no penalty.  Most unusual is that the person writing the book also cooks the menu it accompanies. Tom Fahey combines those roles at Terrace Rooms & Wine on the Isle of Wight; Delfini joins that small club, leaving the pass to pour and explain before returning to finish dishes. He speaks about wine in kitchen terms: acidity cleanses, bitterness refreshes and texture can matter as much as aroma.  The four- and six-wine flights cost £80 and £120 and remain undisclosed until poured, preserving an element of surprise. The upper reaches are impressive but rarely irresistible. Château Margaux 2001 at £950 and Haut-Brion 2001 at £1,100 confirm that maturity and prestige are already present. What is missing is a more persuasive route into them. A premium pairing would allow Delfini to open the cellar’s finest bottles without requiring one table to shoulder the entire cost. 

Dishes

Abruzzo-born Stefano Di Giosia spent more than four years within Heston Blumenthal’s Fat Duck Group, including a year in development, before 18 months at KOL. He cited an Italian maxim that “service is 60% of the experience and the kitchen 40%”. The arithmetic may be debatable; the principle was not. Di Giosia, sous chef Luca Delfini and the wider team repeatedly left the pass to introduce dishes and pairings before returning to cook.  Balfour Leslie’s Reserve Rosé, in Spiegelau Definition stemware, opened the pairing with red fruit, brioche and dry honey. A clear tomato broth paid homage to Tudor potage. White soy supplied the seasoning; charcoal oil provided the impression of food cooked over fire. Three canapés arrived alongside. A crown-shaped taco of coronation chicken managed three references at once: Great Fosters’ royal history through its form and velvet-lined jewellery box, Elizabeth II’s 1953 coronation through its filling, and Di Giosia’s time at KOL through the taco itself. Cured chalk stream trout came on crisp, seaweed-enriched Abruzzese pastry with pickled breakfast radishes. A tomato tartlet, served on timber gathered from Windsor Great Park, combined tomato, Tropea onion, Thai basil and sunflower seeds. Mediterranean in accent, every ingredient had been grown in Britain by local farmers, in open fields and greenhouses.  Courgette and cucumber rarely promise excitement. Here, fig leaf, sorrel, pickled cucumber and gooseberries infused with cardamom and star anise produced freshness, sweetness and a useful edge of char. Delfini poured Drouhin-Vaudon Chablis 2024, whose grapefruit, white flowers and saline acidity were required, he said, to “counterattack” the dish’s several acidic elements. An Austrian orange wine had been trialled, then dismissed as “too strong, too aggressive”. Delfini wanted pasta. Di Giosia did not. Their settlement was squid, cooked gently and sliced into tagliatelle-like ribbons, with its barbecued tentacle concealed inside the coil. Fermented British fava-bean paste, almond purée, compressed Granny Smith apple, fennel and barbecued seaweed brought smoke and savouriness, while a crisp made entirely from squid supplied crunch. Bertani Soave Classico 2023 did more than accompany it: white peach and pear yielded to a bitter-almond finish which completed the almond on the plate.  Bread came from a nearby bakery to the kitchen’s recipe: wild farmed flour, potato and rosemary sourdough, hand-stretched polenta grissini sweetened with estate honey, and outstanding whipped butter seasoned with North Welsh salt and preserved wild garlic. The hand-dived Orkney scallop was the meal’s high point, deeply caramelised yet translucent within and resting on sea herbs. “I wanted to make it British,” said Di Giosia of its curry sauce. Preserved gorse flowers provided the coconut-like perfume; magnolia buds stood in for ginger, while Sussex coriander seed and sansho pepper added fragrance. The result resembled a looser, vastly upgraded HP sauce, with N25 caviar contributing salinity and a little welcome excess. Delfini answered with Mönchhof Grand Lay Riesling Trocken 2024 from a Mosel estate tracing its history to 1177. Its conspicuous “DRY” marker removed any doubt about style, while lime zest, lemongrass, ginger and a faint spritz without neutralising the spice. The main course returned Di Giosia to Abruzzo through “transhumance”, the seasonal movement of people and livestock along established pastoral paths. Perfectly pink dry-aged lamb arrived with salted yoghurt, hazelnut, wild water mint and butter flavoured with what Di Giosia called “Scottish sumac”, alongside a skewer recalling arrosticini, the emblematic Abruzzese preparation he described as a resourceful use of mature sheep. A barely dressed wild-herb salad suggested what shepherds might gather en route, while a sauce reduced for what tasted like an eternity almost eclipsed the meat. “We love making sauces,” he said, needlessly but convincingly. Planeta Eruzione 1614 Nerello Mascalese 2020 brought sour cherry, balsamic herbs, wild thyme and bay. The date was not decoration: Etna’s 1614 eruption continued for ten years, the longest recorded, and the vines grow on that lava flow. Served slightly too warm in a Riedel Nebbiolo/Pinot Noir glass, the wine nevertheless remained joyful, fresh and full, its acidity countering the yoghurt while sustaining the lamb. We finished the first pour before the meat appeared; Delfini immediately replenished it.  Fresh and pickled cherries with koji, shallot and toasted-fennel granita formed a nervy first dessert, refreshing rather than merely resetting. The final pairing travelled furthest from conventional wine service. Akashi-Tai Shiraume Ginjo Umeshu accompanied British strawberries, elderflower and white chocolate, the only chocolate Di Giosia permitted on the menu. Its plum, milk chocolate, marzipan and apricot-kernel character made the match feel entirely logical, while the estate’s own plum trees added a quiet local rhyme.  Finally, Di Giosia dispensed with conventional petits fours because, by this stage, “the brain is foggy”. It proved a more satisfying conclusion than another inevitable pâte de fruits. Instead came laminated buttermilk brioche with orange zest, whipped preserve made from the season’s first apricots, and bee pollen. Dense, chewy and best torn and dipped, it was something one actively wanted to finish rather than politely endure. 

Last Sip

Historic walls draw guests to Great Fosters, but Di Giosia and Delfini have given The Tudor Pass an identity independent of them. Since Delfini assumed responsibility, the wine book has become markedly more adventurous and individual. The logical next step is not more bottles, but greater access to the finest ones through a premium pairing capable of showing what the cellar can really do.

Best for:
